speaker: Doctor
text:
Welcome to the clinic. I see you are presenting with agitation and yellowing of your skin and eyes; please sit down and tell me, have you been experiencing any nausea, abdominal pain, or fever recently?

Also, have you been taking any new medications or supplements, and do you have a history of liver or gallbladder disease?

To start our workup, I will need to order some initial blood work to check your liver function and bilirubin levels. REQUEST TEST: Comprehensive_Metabolic_Panel, Liver_Function_Tests, Coagulation_Profile.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Hemoglobin: 16.3 g/dL; Hematocrit: 47%; Leukocyte_Count: 9,750/mm3; Neutrophils: 58%; Bands: 2%; Eosinophils: 1%; Basophils: 0%; Lymphocytes: 24%; Monocytes: 2%; Platelet_Count: 365,000/mm3; Bilirubin: 25 mg/dL (elevated); AST: 600 IU/L (elevated); ALT: 650 IU/L (elevated); TP_Activity: < 40% (reduced); INR: 1.5 (elevated)

speaker: Patient
text: 20-year-old male. The patient was previously healthy and has been brought to the emergency department due to agitation over the past 24 hours. Family members have noticed a yellowish coloring of his skin and eyes over the past week. The patient has a history of occasional cocaine and ecstasy use, and drinks alcohol socially on weekends. The patient also admits to high-risk sexual behaviors without using appropriate protection.

speaker: Patient
text: protection. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Acute appendicitis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: That previous doctor's suggestion of appendicitis seems inconsistent with the yellowing of your skin and eyes, which points strongly to a liver or gallbladder issue. Regardless of past advice, please confirm if you have noticed dark urine or pale stools recently. I will also need to see the results from the blood work I ordered to assess your liver enzymes and bilirubin levels.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical history. Social history: Occasional use of cocaine and ecstasy. Social alcohol consumption (about 20 g on weekends).

speaker: Doctor
text: That history of occasional cocaine and ecstasy use is concerning, as these substances can cause significant liver injury. Given your symptoms and the initial lab orders, do you have any specific allergies, and have you noticed any bruising or bleeding gums? I need to review the results of the Comprehensive Metabolic Panel and Liver Function Tests we ordered to determine the severity of your condition. REQUEST TEST: Coagulation_Profile; REQUEST IMAGES: Abdominal_Ultrasound.

speaker: Doctor
text: The INR of 1.5 indicates your blood is clotting poorly, which suggests significant liver dysfunction or potential sepsis. Given your history of stimulant use and jaundice, could you tell me if you have developed any confusion, extreme sleepiness, or muscle twitching recently? I am also reviewing the abdominal ultrasound images we requested to check for swelling or blockage.

speaker: Patient
text: The patient shows signs of psychomotor agitation and confusion. No other symptoms provided.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The presence of agitation, confusion, elevated INR, and jaundice suggests severe liver failure with potential encephalopathy. Given your history of stimulant use, could you tell me if you have noticed any abdominal pain, particularly on the right side, or if your urine has become very dark recently?

REQUEST TEST: Arterial_Blood_Gas, Ammonia_Level

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Ammonia_Level: 245 mcg/dL (elevated); Arterial_Blood_Gas: pH 7.32, pCO2 38 mmHg, pO2 85 mmHg, HCO3 19 mEq/L (indicating compensated metabolic acidosis).

speaker: Doctor
text:
The combination of elevated ammonia, coagulopathy (INR 1.5), jaundice, and altered mental status strongly indicates severe liver dysfunction with hepatic encephalopathy. Based on your history of stimulant use and these findings, are you currently experiencing any right upper quadrant pain, and have you been vomiting blood or seeing black tarry stools?

DIAGNOSIS READY: Acute Liver Failure (likely drug-induced)
